I turn now to my own history. Of its earliest portion there is little to tell, and I shall be brief; yet I must linger somewhat over my childhood, so that it may be understood why, with the failure of one hope, all life must become empty, and why the ruin of the sole affection I was allowed to nourish extinguished my existence also.

I have remarked how little my aunt resembled my father. I believe that, without the faintest touch of wickedness, hers was the coldest heart ever lodged in a human bosom, wholly incapable of attachment. She undertook my protection because she held it to be her duty; but she had spent too many years alone, free from children’s chatter and noise, to suffer me to interrupt her peace. She had never married, and for the preceding five years had lived entirely by herself on an estate inherited through her mother, beside Loch Lomond in Scotland. In his letters my father had wished her to live with me at the family mansion, in a lovely district near Richmond in Yorkshire. She refused this arrangement. As soon as she had settled the business that her brother’s departure had placed in her hands, she left England and carried me to her Scottish property.

Through infancy and until my eighth year, I was cared for by a servant of my mother’s, who had joined us in our retirement for that purpose. My rooms lay in a distant part of the house, and I saw my aunt only at appointed times. These visits came twice daily: about noon she entered my nursery, and after dinner I was brought to her. She never offered me a caress, and throughout my presence seemed apprehensive that some childish trick would disturb her. Before venturing into the parlour, my kind nurse instructed me with the utmost care. The fear inspired by my aunt’s chill expression and scant, constrained speech was so powerful that I seldom discredited those lessons or abandoned the exemplary quiet I had been taught to maintain on these brief occasions.

Under my good nurse’s guardianship I wandered freely through our park and the adjoining fields. Born of the deepest love, I showed from my first years a nature of extreme sensibility. I cannot express the passionate affection I felt for everything around me, even for objects without life.

Emma had no cause to repent having condescended to visit the Coles. Next day the evening supplied her with many agreeable recollections; and whatever she might have sacrificed in dignified reserve must have been repaid abundantly by the brilliance of her popularity. She must have given the Coles great pleasure—worthy people, who merited happiness!—and left behind a reputation that would not quickly fade.

Complete happiness is uncommon even in recollection, however, and two matters troubled her a little. She wondered whether, in disclosing to Frank Churchill her suspicions about Jane Fairfax’s affections, she had failed in the duty one woman owed another. It was scarcely proper; yet the notion had taken such hold that it would slip out. His acceptance of everything she said paid so flattering a tribute to her insight that she could hardly convince herself she ought to have kept silent.

Her second regret likewise concerned Jane Fairfax, and on this point she felt no uncertainty. She sincerely and decidedly regretted that her own singing and playing were inferior. She lamented most earnestly the idleness of her childhood—and seated herself to practise diligently for an hour and a half.

Harriet’s arrival interrupted her; and had Harriet’s admiration been sufficient, she would soon have found consolation.

“Oh, if only I could play as you and Miss Fairfax do!”

“Do not put us together, Harriet. My playing resembles hers no more than lamplight resembles sunshine.”

“Oh, dear! I think you are the better player. I think you play every bit as well as she does. Certainly I would much sooner listen to you. Everybody yesterday evening remarked how beautifully you played.”

“Anyone who understood the matter must have noticed the difference. The fact is, Harriet, that I play just well enough to receive compliments, while Jane Fairfax is far beyond that.”

“Well, I shall always believe you play equally well, or that nobody could ever detect any difference. Mr. Cole spoke of your excellent taste, and Mr. Frank Churchill said a great deal about it too. He said he prized taste much more highly than execution.”

“Ah, Harriet, but Jane Fairfax possesses both.”

“Are you certain? I noticed her execution, but never knew she had taste. No one mentioned it. Besides, I cannot bear Italian singing—you cannot understand a single word. And if she plays so remarkably well, it is only what she is obliged to do, you know, since she will have to teach.

I thought this peculiar lie had been told with remarkable simplicity and beauty. But I had heard it only once, which makes a difference. No doubt the others had enjoyed it when it was new.

Sir Dinadan the Humorist woke first and soon stirred everyone else with a thoroughly poor practical joke. He tied metal mugs to a dog’s tail and let him loose. The terrified animal raced round and round, with every other dog barking in pursuit. They crashed into whatever stood in their way, producing utter confusion and a deafening racket. Every man and woman present laughed until tears ran down their faces; some tumbled from their chairs and rolled on the floor in delight. They were like a crowd of children. Sir Dinadan was so pleased with himself that he kept explaining, to the point of exhaustion, how this immortal idea had come to him. Like others of his brand of comedian, he was still laughing long after everyone else had finished. His success inflated him enough to attempt a speech—a funny one, naturally. I don't think I have ever heard so many worn-out jokes strung together. He was worse than the minstrels, worse than a circus clown. There was something especially depressing about sitting thirteen hundred years before my birth and hearing those same feeble, flat, moth-eaten jokes that had made me sick as a boy thirteen hundred years later. I nearly became convinced that a genuinely new joke was impossible. Everyone laughed at these ancient relics—but people always do. I had noticed that centuries afterward. The scoffer, of course, did not laugh; I mean the boy. He scoffed instead. Nothing was safe from his scorn. He said most of Sir Dinadan’s jokes were rotten and the rest fossilized. I told him “fossilized” was good, since I too believed that only geological periods could do justice to the impressive age of some of them. But this neat idea found no foothold in his mind: geology had yet to be invented. Still, I made a note of the remark and planned to educate the nation enough to appreciate it, assuming I survived. No point throwing away a good thing just because the market is not ready.

Then Sir Kay rose and started up his storytelling machine, using me as fuel.
